title: A checkpoint gene and tumor growth

stimulus.title: Mice with zero, one or two working copies of gene T
stimulus.html:
Gene T codes for a protein needed at the G2 checkpoint: it stops cells with damaged DNA from entering mitosis. Researchers bred mice with two working copies of gene T, one working copy, or no working copies (both copies disabled). Experiment 1: 30 mice of each kind were checked every month for tumors. Experiment 2: skin cells from each kind of mouse were grown in culture, exposed to a dose of X-rays that breaks DNA, and the percentage of cells entering mitosis in the next 2 hours was measured in 4 cultures each. Unexposed cells were measured in the same way.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt:
(i) Describe what the G2 checkpoint checks before a cell enters mitosis.
(ii) Explain how cyclin and a cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) together move a cell from G2 into mitosis.

rubric.point: (i) Describes that the G2 checkpoint checks that the DNA has been completely copied and is not damaged (cell size may also be mentioned).
accept: whether all DNA is replicated and undamaged
checks for DNA damage and complete copying before mitosis

rubric.point: (ii) Explains that mitotic cyclin builds up and binds the CDK, activating it; the active cyclin-CDK (MPF) phosphorylates target proteins that start mitosis (for example condensing chromosomes, breaking down the nuclear envelope).
accept: cyclin binds and activates CDK, which phosphorylates proteins that trigger mitosis
rising cyclin activates CDK, a kinase whose targets start mitosis
the cyclin-CDK complex (MPF) adds phosphates to proteins that drive the cell into M

parts.sample: (i) The G2 checkpoint checks that all of the DNA has been copied and that it is not damaged before the cell can enter mitosis. (ii) Mitotic cyclin builds up during S and G2 and binds its CDK, which is inactive on its own. The active cyclin-CDK complex (MPF) is a kinase that phosphorylates target proteins, and those phosphorylated proteins start mitosis: the chromosomes condense and the nuclear envelope breaks down.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt:
(i) Identify the independent variable in experiment 1.
(ii) Identify the purpose of measuring unexposed cells in experiment 2.
(iii) State the null hypothesis for comparing cells with two working copies and cells with no working copies of gene T after X-rays in experiment 2.

rubric.point: (i) The number of working copies of gene T (0, 1 or 2).
accept: how many working copies of gene T the mice have

rubric.point: (ii) To show the normal rate of entering mitosis without DNA damage, so a drop after X-rays can be attributed to the X-rays (and to show the three kinds of cells divide at the same rate when undamaged).
accept: a control showing the baseline rate of mitosis without X-rays
shows any difference after X-rays is due to the damage, not to the cells dividing at different rates anyway

rubric.point: (iii) There is no difference in the percentage of cells entering mitosis after X-rays between cells with two working copies and cells with no working copies of gene T.
accept: the number of copies of gene T has no effect on the percentage of irradiated cells entering mitosis
any difference between the two groups is due to chance

parts.sample: (i) The independent variable is the number of working copies of gene T: two, one or none. (ii) The unexposed cells show how often each kind of cell enters mitosis without DNA damage. All three are about 6%, so the low values in exposed cells with gene T can be attributed to the X-ray damage, not to those cells simply dividing less. (iii) Null hypothesis: the percentage of X-rayed cells entering mitosis is the same for cells with two working copies and cells with no working copies of gene T.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt:
(i) Calculate how many more mice with no working copies than mice with two working copies had a tumor by 12 months.
(ii) Using the error bars (±2 SE), determine whether the percentage of X-rayed cells entering mitosis differs significantly between cells with one and two working copies of gene T. Support your answer.

rubric.point: (i) 26 more mice: 90% of 30 = 27 and 3% of 30 ≈ 1 (the percentages are rounded: 1 of 30 is 3.3%), so 27 − 1 = 26.
(ii) Not significantly different: one copy 0.9 ± 0.4 gives 0.5-1.3, two copies 0.4 ± 0.3 gives 0.1-0.7; the intervals overlap (0.5-0.7), so the data do not show a difference.
accept: the ±2 SE ranges overlap, so no significant difference
0.5-1.3 and 0.1-0.7 overlap, so the difference may be due to chance

parts.sample: (i) No working copies: 90% of 30 = 27 mice. Two working copies: 3% of 30 = 0.9, which is 1 mouse (1 of 30 is 3.3%, rounded to 3%). 27 − 1 = 26 more mice. (ii) Cells with one copy: 0.9 ± 0.4, or 0.5 to 1.3%. Cells with two copies: 0.4 ± 0.3, or 0.1 to 0.7%. The intervals overlap between 0.5 and 0.7%, so the data do not show a significant difference: one working copy is enough to hold most damaged cells at the checkpoint.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt:
(i) Support the claim that gene T is a tumor suppressor gene, using evidence from both experiments.
(ii) Mice with one working copy develop tumors later than mice with none, even though their cells hold at the checkpoint almost as well as cells with two copies. Explain why tumors still develop in these mice, and why later.

rubric.point: (i) Uses both experiments: without gene T, damaged cells still enter mitosis at the normal rate (6.2%, the same as unexposed) instead of being held at the checkpoint, and mice without gene T develop far more tumors, sooner (57% by 6 months against 0%); so gene T's protein stops division of damaged cells, which is the job of a tumor suppressor.
accept: losing gene T lets damaged cells divide (experiment 2) and leads to more tumors (experiment 1)
gene T normally halts damaged cells; mice lacking it get tumors early, as expected for a tumor suppressor

rubric.point: (ii) Explains that a cell in these mice loses the checkpoint only when its remaining working copy is also disabled by a new mutation; this second change happens in few cells and takes time, so tumors appear later than in mice whose cells all lack gene T from the start.
accept: a tumor needs the second copy to be lost by a later mutation, which takes time
one working copy is enough until a mutation disables it in some cell; that cell can then divide with damaged DNA and give rise to a tumor

parts.sample: (i) In experiment 2, X-rayed cells with gene T almost stop entering mitosis (0.4-0.9%), but cells with no working copies keep entering mitosis at the normal rate (6.2%, like unexposed cells): without gene T, damaged cells are not stopped. In experiment 1, mice with no working copies get tumors much sooner and more often (57% by 6 months, 100% by 18) than mice with two copies (0% and 7%). A gene whose protein stops damaged cells from dividing, and whose loss leads to tumors, is a tumor suppressor. (ii) In mice with one working copy, each cell still makes enough T protein to hold damaged cells at the checkpoint. A tumor can start only in a cell whose remaining working copy is disabled by a new mutation. That second change happens by chance in only a few cells and takes time, so tumors appear later (13% at 12 months, 47% at 18) than in mice whose cells lack gene T from birth.
